items.title: DOJ Election Interference Turns Into Raw Thuggery
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
I have the same mix of feelings that I did in the days leading up to Jan. 6, 2021: a queasy feeling that things are about to spiral out of control along with the recognition that it could end up just being a clown show.

The Justice Department’s corrupt, heavy-handed, intimidation tactics of issuing grand jury subpoenas to election officials in California while launching a wave of new election-related subpoenas in Alaska is a level of thuggery we haven’t seen before and a grave threat.

The only more direct and dramatic interference in free and fair elections would be blocking voter access to the polls, seizing ballots, and refusing to abide by the results of the election. Stay tuned, I guess?

And yet there remains an unmistakable clownish quality to the whole endeavor, such as Attorney General Todd Blanche personally charging four misdemeanor cases in Nevada for alleged noncitizen voting, presumably because the top federal prosecutor in the state is implicated in the Trump U.S. attorney scheme and was disqualified.

It is, as always, both/and.

Trump DOJ Ignores Judges Warning

In California, the Trump DOJ reportedly made the decision to target election officials themselves with a new round of grand jury subpoenas, Bloomberg reports:

Justice Department leadership directed top federal prosecutors in California to pursue criminal subpoenas of state and local officials regarding their roles administering allegedly illegal voting, according to two people familiar with the situation.

This is different from earlier grand jury subpoenas in recent weeks that were directed at obtaining voting records to prosecute alleged noncitizen voting. The new subpoenas are going directly to election officials who are in the midst of counting votes and managing an election.

The new subpoenas aren’t limited just to Los Angeles County: “All four U.S. attorneys in California were issuing subpoenas, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation,” the AP reported.

The subpoenas come after acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to election officials in every California county earlier this month warning that they faced potential criminal prosecution for counting the ballots of alleged noncitizen voters — an unprecedented interpretation of federal criminal law.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, echoed those threats in court this week.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter warned from the bench Tuesday that DOJ’s threats against election officials needed to “cease immediately.”

In his order rejecting the Trump DOJ’s request that he order Los Angeles County to segregate and not yet count alleged mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters, Judge Carter warned DOJ again: “The court reiterates what it said yesterday: these threats must stop.”

The next day came with word of the new round of subpoenas.

Conflicting Reports on Timing of Subpoenas

Not all of the reporting is consistent as to when subpoenas were issued and served. But it appears that some subpoenas of election workers went out as early as last week.

“At least two employees of Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office received grand jury subpoenas last week for a proceeding scheduled for Nov. 4, on the morning after the election,” the NYT reported.

Three subpoenas to employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder were sent Oct. 21 and 24, according to the AP, which obtained copies of them:

The subpoenas request any documents and communications related to letters sent in July and October by federal officials to state election officials outlining allegations of noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls. … They also seek any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted.

Those subpoenas predate the new wave of subpoenas that reportedly began yesterday in all four federal district in California.

Again, the focus of these latest subpoenas is different than a separate batch of prior subpoenas that focused on getting voting records in order to prosecute individual voters for allegedly being noncitizens. One such subpoena was received by Orange County election officials yesterday, adding to the confusion.

Grand jury subpoenas days before the election is intimidation enough, but there was at least one extra twist: “Federal marshals served one county employee at home, despite having already served that employee at the registrar’s office and issuing a notification of counsel, according to officials familiar with the incident,” the NYT reports.

“Threats and intimidation have no place in elections,” said Dean Logan, the top election official in Los Angeles County.

Wave of Subpoenas in Alaska

Further seizing on the NYT report that tied the candidacy of the Dan Sullivan to the Senate campaign of Mary Peltola, the Trump DOJ issued a wave of new subpoenas ostensibly to investigate what it claims is a conspiracy to deceive voters — but which is in reality a last-ditch effort to save a key incumbent Republican senator.

“Federal prosecutors issued more than 40 grand jury subpoenas and record preservation notices to key targets by [Wednesday] evening, one of the officials said,” according to CNN, which reported that additional subpoenas were expected yesterday.

There had already been a quiet federal investigation of the Sullivan candidacy before the NYT story, with some grand jury subpoenas issued and witnesses interviewed, CNN reported:

The investigation had already roiled the US Attorney’s office in Alaska, one of the officials said, where some career prosecutors have balked at aspects of the probe and whether the effort broke federal law or simply represents electioneering dirty tricks.

It seems clear now that the NYT report embarrassed officials at Main Justice since the newspaper story went farther than its own investigation had.

In a move I’ve never seen before, the Alaska U.S. attorney Michael Heyman “un-recused” himself from the case after the NYT report at the urging of Main Justice, CNN reported. Heyman had previously recused himself early in the probe because he was in discussions with Sens. Dan Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski about being nominated for a federal judgeship.

The prosecutor-in-chief made clear his intentions soon after the NYT story broke: “I think they should be prosecuted,” President Trump said. “To me, that’s voter fraud at the highest level.”

Trump: Why Is MY Beak Dry?!?

Special Weekend Morning Memo

Keep an eye on your inbox for a special weekend edition of Morning Memo.

With the campaigns chugging to the finish line and Trump election interference in full swing, Morning Memo will bring you the latest. Stay tuned …

items.title: Trump Is on an Absurd Collision Course With Yet Another Federal Judge
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Trump DOJ’s No. 3 Official in the Hot Seat

A golf course in D.C. is the improbable venue for another significant Trump II showdown between the executive and judicial branches.

Unlike, say, the Alien Enemies Act, Abrego Garcia, and immigrant habeas cases, where the actions that precipitated the conflict between the Trump administration and federal judges were unmistakably serious deprivations of liberty, the East Potomac Golf Course case has layers of absurdism, which we’ll get into below.

My main reason for catching you up on this second-tier constitutional confrontation is to preview an important hearing in the case tomorrow, so that I can come back to this later without burdening you with a whole bunch of backstory.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes had already ordered the Trump DOJ to show cause by yesterday why it should not be ordered to preserve all records in the case in what could only be interpreted as a prelude to her considering sanctions against government lawyers for allegedly misleading her. Reyes was particularly focused on the Trump DOJ’s failure to comply with her orders to provide sufficient notice of the surprise removal of hundreds of trees on the golf course over the Columbus Day weekend.

But now Judge Reyes has a new bone to pick with the Trump DOJ.

Judge Reyes has suspected that the mass tree removal over the holiday weekend was part of Trump’s plan to remake the historic golf course without congressional approval — but the administration and DOJ lawyers have denied it, repeatedly and emphatically.

Then on Tuesday, on her own, Judge Reyes took judicial notice of a new Truth Social post by President Trump, in which he declared that the golf course will be closing on Nov. 15, and demanded to know why the Trump DOJ had previously told her otherwise:

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward told the Court on October 19 that “[w]ith regard to the November 15th date… there is no plan to close the course.” The Court ORDERS Defendants to clarify, as part of their response to the Court’s show-cause order from October 26, whether any plan exists to close East Potomac Golf Course on or around November 15, 2026. And, if so, how that can be reconciled with Associate AG Woodward’s representation to the Court.

In her order, Reyes also scheduled a “status hearing” for Friday and ordered Woodward — who represented Trump’s co-defendants in the Mar-a-Lago case and Jan. 6 rioters — to appear at the hearing in person. The DOJ’s No. 3 personally handling cases is unheard of, let alone doing the president’s dirty work. Getting hauled into court for allegedly misleading a judge is beyond next level stuff.

Yesterday, in his response to the court order, Woodward conceded that there is a plan to close the golf course, but he did not reconcile his prior statements to the contrary:

The undersigned acknowledges the President has twice directed Interior and the National Park Service to close the park by November 15. Accordingly, Interior, acting through counsel, is working to develop a plan to implement that direction and will provide this Court with notice pursuant to the Court’s October 26, 2026, Order.

That prompted another stern order from Judge Reyes ahead of tomorrow’s hearing, which she has now recast as a show cause hearing that is quite a bit broader than merely whether the Trump DOJ must preserve documents in the case:

The Court ORDERS the Government to come prepared to state at the hearing: (1) whether it continues to maintain that there is no final agency action; (2) the dates and times at which President Trump “twice directed Interior and the National Park Service to close the park by November 15”; … and (3) the first date “Interior, acting through counsel” began “working to develop a plan to implement that direction,” id. Associate Attorney General Woodward remains ORDERED to appear at the hearing in person. The Court FURTHER ORDERS the attendance of at least one counsel from the Department of the Interior’s Office of the Solicitor with pre-existing experience on this case.

Shortly thereafter, Woodward provided the court-required detailed notice of the administration’s plan to shut down the vast majority of East Potomac Park, including the golf course, even though the renovation plan at issue will not have been approved yet on the administration’s own timetable.

The ostensible reason for closing the golf course before getting approval for the renovation is familiar: “significant safety hazards.” It’s similar to the pretext offered for the separate closure of the Kennedy Center, another D.C. public asset that Trump has tried to turn into a personal project. In this case, the public safety hazard is an allegedly “deteriorated sea wall that is currently crumbling into the Potomac River.”

All of this is to tee up tomorrow’s show cause hearing for you. It’s admittedly an odd sideshow in the last week before Election Day. But it wouldn’t be Trump lawlessness without a heaping dose of absurdity.

Trump DOJ Election Interference Watch

: U.S. District Judge David O. Carter late yesterday rejected the Trump DOJ’s request to force Los Angeles County to segregate and not yet count mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters. In a stirring opinion, Judge Carter repeatedly blasted the Trump administration’s interference in California’s election:

Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch. In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.

: The Trump DOJ seized on a NYT investigation that tied the campaign of Mary Peltola to a scheme to add a second Dan Sullivan to the ballot. In a new filing by DOJ No. 3 official Stan Woodward, he withdrew his prior opposition to the Peltola campaign and the DSCC intervening in the DOJ lawsuit to block certification of the Senate election. Instead, Woodward said DOJ would use expedited discovery in the case to investigate the alleged “sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up a sham candidate for the purpose of deceiving Alaskan voters” and whether the Peltola campaign “attempted to deceive” the court. UCLA election law expert Rick Hasen assesses the legal implications of this whole mess.

: Secretary of State Steve Hobbs told the Trump DOJ that its purported list of 400 alleged noncitizen voters contained actual U.S. citizens. In a letter, Hobbs said it would “irresponsible and illegal” to segregate and not yet count mail-in ballots from voters on the Trump DOJ list.

SPLC Reveals Its Theory of the Case Against It

The Southern Poverty Law Center has revealed in a new filing its theory of how the vindictive prosecution of it by the Trump administration came to be.

The civil rights group alleges that the Trump DOJ — which has zeroed in on the SPLC’s former program of using white supremacists as paid informants against other white supremacists — was able to flip the SPLC’s own longest-tenured informant into a government informant against the SPLC because he had failed to pay income taxes for 30 years.

The SPLC alleges that the flipped informant practically became a member of the prosecution team, with numerous meetings and 1,800 text messages between him and investigators over the last year. Identified in the filing as “F-9,” the informant also provided documents, reports, and four so-called “Intelligence Briefings” to investigators, the SPLC alleges:

To be clear, F-9 should have been merely a in this case. But the government has treated him like part of the prosecutorial team itself, choosing to allow F-9 to decide which of the documents, recordings, and photographs in his possession he will produce, and how and when he will produce them. F-9 admitted that he has a “house full of documents,” some of which he has referenced plans to “shred.”

The immediate purpose of the SPLC’s new filing was to obtain permission to subpoena the informant and obtain a court order for the informant to preserve the materials in his possession.

Quote of the Day: Transformers Edition

“The Arch is a generational national defense opportunity to mitigate these evolving threats. It will be utilized as a dual-purpose structure: a major national monument that also incorporates military utility to support Homeland defense.”—

items.title: The Trump DOJ’s OTHER Scheme to Interfere in the Midterm Elections
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
The Retribution: Election Interference Edition

The Trump DOJ’s unprecedented moves to stop ballot-counting and election certification are its most direct interference in the midterms — but it’s also bootstrapping in its long-running scheme of retribution against Trump foes in service of partisan campaign narratives while voting is underway.

By timing prosecutions and overt investigative steps to maximize their pre-election impact, the Trump DOJ is not merely ignoring long-standing department policy about avoiding the public impression of election meddling. It’s actively abusing the powers of the federal government by using federal law enforcement for partisan ends. It’s happening broadly under the auspices of DOJ, but Department of Homeland Security law enforcement components are also involved.

I had intended to write about this dynamic this morning anyway, and then the NYT and WaPo each published versions of the same story. I’d recommend both of them. Here are the recent cases most directly tied to complementing and reinforcing Trump campaign rhetoric while voting is underway:

  • : The Trump DOJ tried to indict the star witness of the Jan. 6 Committee yesterday — exactly one week before Election Day — but was rebuffed by a D.C. grand jury.

  • 2 FBI agents in Hunter Biden case: The first inkling of the no-true bill in the Hutchinson case came during a raucous hearing on concerns about a highly politicized and problematic new prosecution of two FBI agents involved in the Hunter Biden investigation. The flimsy case was thrown together on orders from FBI Director Kash Patel and was perceived inside the bureau as a political “witch hunt,” a key FBI witness testified yesterday. The case was first charged on Friday.

  • : The Oct. 5 timing of Trump II’s criminal case against former FBI Director James Comey — which was unsealed this week at Comey’s request — seems to have been driven at least by an expiring statute of limitations, not solely the election. But they’re not mutually exclusive, of course. Like in the case against the FBI agents above, DOJ proceeded to file charges against Comey without a grand jury indictment.

  • : The Oct. 12 HSI raid on the private D.C. residence of a sitting Democratic member of Congress, who also is a Black woman of Somali heritage, managed to be brazen retribution and to mirror President Trump’s persistent racist targeting of Black women and Somali Americans.

  • Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas (D): On Oct. 14, the Trump DOJ indicted the President pro tempore of the Virginia Senate on allegations that her family set up an illegal marijuana business. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel held a press conference announcing the indictment.

  • : The FBI yesterday raided the Beverly Hill mansion of billionaire and former Democratic donor Stephen Cloobeck, reportedly a close associate of former Rep. Eric Swalwell. The NYT reports that the raid came as part of an ongoing investigation into sexual misconduct allegations.

The key is timing. Even where there might arguably be properly predicated investigations and prosecutions, the decision to proceed in high profile public ways before the election is a — notwithstanding Blanche’s feeble protests to the contrary.

A great visualization from the WaPo of the abuse of federal law enforcement in service of GOP election rhetoric around the Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting:

Awaiting Ruling in CA Election Case …

As I reported late yesterday, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter of Los Angeles said he will rule today on the Trump DOJ’s request for a TRO to segregate and not yet count ballots from a list of some 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters.

During a 3 1/2-hour hearing on the TRO, Judge Carter appeared likely to kick the core of the case past Election Day, thereby thwarting the Trump DOJ and minimizing the worst impacts of its effort to interfere in the election.

Bill Essayli Disqualified AGAIN

For the second time, a federal judge has found that Bill Essayli is unlawfully serving as the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles. Essayli was slotted into the role as part of the broader Trump scheme to install loyalists as federal prosecutors in blue states, bypassing the Senate and defying federal law.

Essayli was previously disqualified by U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright of Hawaii from handling certain criminal cases as acting U.S. attorney because he overstayed his term in that role. Essayli was allowed to stay on as first assistant U.S. attorney and assumed all the duties of a regular U.S. attorney.

But subsequent appeals court decisions in others cases have more thoroughly blocked the workaround that President Trump and the DOJ used to install Essayli, so in a new ruling Judge Seabright tightened his previous decision even more. The most immediate impact will be to keep Essayli from managing or overseeing attorneys in the specific criminal cases where his appointment was challenged. Seabright gave Essayli a chance to appeal before the ruling goes into effect.

Ironically, Essayli personally argued the administration’s side in the California election case on the same day Seabright found him to be unlawfully serving.

The Ongoing Coverup of the Alex Pretti Killing

As Morning Memo first reported two weeks ago, despite what publicly looked like a breakthrough in July, the Trump administration has continued to stonewall Minnesota authorities trying to investigate the three ICE shootings during Operation Metro Surge.

Yesterday, the parents of Alex Pretti, one of the two U.S. citizens killed by ICE in January, held a press conference deploring the Trump DOJ’s conduct since the shooting of their son.

“Our son was murdered. We all saw it. And the lack of cooperation is baffling, it’s disappointing and reprehensible,” his father said.

A Confounding Read: DOGE Edition

Wired: A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There

items.title: 3 Big Losses for Trump in One Long Day of Setbacks
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Yesterday was another extraordinary day on the political-legal front, with few commonalities among the three major rulings to knit them together into a coherent whole — except that the Trump administration consistently lost.

Trump’s losses came across a wide-range of purported assertions of executive power. He was blocked from:

  • interfering in California’s state-run federal elections;

  • firing career federal prosecutor Maurene Comey in disregard of civil service protections; and

  • disregarding Congress and federal law in pushing forward his personalist golf course project in D.C.

But set against those losses you still had corrupt new assertions of executive power:

  • vindictively prosecuting Maurene Comey’s father, the former FBI director James Comey, for the time.

You can see some connecting threads there, of course: the use of the Big Lie of noncitizen voting to undermine an election that Republicans are expected to lose badly, and the ongoing campaign of retribution against the Comey family for the supposed sins of the father.

It is also implicitly a story of the federal judiciary stiffening its spine, albeit unevenly, in the face of outrageous conduct by the Trump administration both in and out of court.

There’s a lot to unpack here, as the pace of Trump malfeasance quickens ahead of the election.

Harmonic Convergence of Trump Schemes

I do want to tie together two Trump schemes that have now become intertwined.

For months, I’ve been banging on here about President Trump’s scheme to circumvent the Senate, the Constitution, and federal law to install loyalists as the top federal prosecutors in blue states.

The scheme itself is lawless enough in its own right, but I’ve warned that it’s not an end unto itself, but a potential means to other bad acts, like targeting elected Dems.

Now we’re seeing at least one aspect of the end game coming into view: election interference.

Trump’s scheme to use the Big Lie of noncitizen voting to interfere in the midterm elections is being unspooled first in three districts that each have top federal prosecutors who were installed as part of Trump’s U.S. attorney scheme: the Central District of California and now the Eastern and Western Districts of Washington state.

Both Bill Essayli in Los Angeles and Pete Serrano in Spokane were installed as top prosecutors via a backdoor workaround that courts in other districts have already shot down as unlawful. Charles Neil Floyd in Seattle was installed after Trump fired court-appointed U.S. Attorney Roger Rogoff (who is suing over his termination), another Trump DOJ method that other courts have already invalidated. In addition to Rogoff’s lawsuit, litigation has already been underway challenging the appointment of Essayli.

Essayli has taken a high-profile public role in pushing the administration’s use of the pretext of noncitizen voting to interfere in the midterm elections. Serrano and Floyd followed suit yesterday with public fanfare. While the Big Lie scheme is being driven by top political appointees at Main Justice, all three prosecutors have made public pronouncements, and Essayli has facilitated arrests and prosecutions of alleged noncitizen voters.

It’s harder to imagine pulling off the scheme to interfere in the midterms with independent U.S. attorneys in place who came into office in the usual lawful ways: either Senate-confirmed after blue-slip approval from home state Democratic senators, or as career first assistant U.S. attorneys, or as federal court appointees.

The different lawful ways of installing a permanent or acting U.S. attorney speak to the checks and balances in place to preserve the separation of powers, pitting the legislative and judicial branches against the executive branch in a purposeful tension.

Trump has run roughshod over those checks and balances, and while the courts have repeatedly rejected his U.S. attorney scheme, they’ve been too slow to prevent the scheme from having real-world impacts on the election.

9th Circuit Blocks CA Election Interference

In a major early ruling, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Trump DOJ’s scheme to make California segregate and not count mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters.

The 2-1 decision, which I write about at length here, found the Trump DOJ appeal to be premature and left the court without appellate jurisdiction to even hear it. But the dissent by a Trump appointee who reached the merits of the case prompted the two judges in the majority to file separate concurrences that said they would have ruled against the Trump DOJ had they had jurisdiction.

The two concurring opinions did two things: (i) laid out a map for the trial judge who is now considering the merits of the case what the appeals court panel will tolerate; and (ii) signaled to the Trump DOJ that it will be unlikely to prevail when the case returns to the 9th Circuit on the merits.

Notably, neither the Trump DOJ or any other judge on the 9th Circuit sought a rehearing last night of the panel’s decision. Unless the Trump DOJ goes to the Supreme Court next (and a clearly premature appeal would be a terrible posture from which to seek high court intervention), the case resumes today with an important hearing in front of U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who is in the somewhat unusual position of first taking up a case after it’s already been up on appeal.

California Case Gets Even Wackier

Ahead of today’s hearing in Los Angeles, the Trump DOJ filed new declarations overnight. Two things jump out, and they’re both doozies:

  • The Trump DOJ filed a declaration in support of its case from none other than Clint Curtis, the top election official in Shasta County who offered a job in his office to Big Lie aficionado Tina Peters after she was released from prison in Colorado. Peters declined the job. Curtis, who was defeated for reelection in June by someone he fired, claims that based on his knowledge of county election systems Los Angeles County can easily segregate alleged noncitizen ballots as the Trump DOJ is demanding.

  • In the course of challenging Los Angeles County’s preliminary analysis of the DOJ’s list of alleged noncitizen voter, a DHS official’s declaration appears to concede that one of the voters on the DOJ list turned out to be deceased and that four others “might have a claim to U.S. citizenship.”

The Trump DOJ’s attempt to block the certification of the U.S. Senate election in Alaska sits in a different bucket than the Big Lie of noncitizen voting. This is an opportunistic effort to salvage a seat based on the potential confusion around two candidates names, one of whom is the incumbent Republican — but it has the usual hallmarks of Trump DOJ lawlessness and sloppiness.

  • The state of Alaska defendants have responded to the DOJ’s lawsuit for the first time and are opposing it. They filed a motion to dismiss.

  • Chief Judge Sharon L. Gleason (Obama) granted a motion to expedite her ruling on whether to allow Alaskans for Mary, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, and other third parties to intervene in the case. She set a briefing schedule on that motion and, in the event she allows them to intervene, on the intervenor’s motions to dismiss.

  • In her order, Judge Gleason put enough spin on the ball to suggest she’s skeptical of the DOJ’s case. Among the clues she dropped, Judge Gleason noted that the general election ballot layout is the same as the one used in the primary and then wryly remarked: “The Court is unaware of any legal challenge as to how either candidate was listed on the primary ballot.”

  • Judge Gleason also offered up this accurate but hardly neutral description of how we got here: “After Alaskans had already begun casting their ballots for the November 2026 election—and nearly four months after the Alaska Supreme Court directed the Division of Elections to include Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot for the upcoming United States Senate election—the United States initiated this action on October 22, 2026.”

The Biggest Pre-Election Concern

There is a dangerous possibility that the California and Alaska lawsuits may be precursors for a search warrant to seize ballots. The federal government has relied on debunked claims of voter fraud in past ballot seizures, like in Fulton County. Given DOJ’s recent track record, the lack of evidence of any actual crime in Alaska or California may not deter the federal government in seeking a warrant.

Trump Offers $1M for Voter Fraud Tips

President Trump, in a social media post: “Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud!”

“This is the first time ever that we have had to engage in scenario planning to safeguard against potential federal interference in elections. It seems like the federal government is now adversarial to the states.”—Shenna Bellows (D), Maine secretary of state

Comey Vindictively Prosecuted Again

Wrongfully Fired Maurene Comey Wins

In a case with big implications for civil service protections and for President Trump’s unlawful purge of the Justice Department, U.S. District Judge Jesse M. Furman of Manhattan ruled in favor of fired career federal prosecutor Maurene Comey in her wrongful termination lawsuit against the DOJ. Another case we could spend all day unpacking. Suffice to say that there’s a lot here that will be tested on appeal. Stay tuned …

A Wild Ruling on Trump’s Golf Course Plan

Most of the headlines are focused on U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes of D.C. blocking the Trump administration from cutting down any more trees on the East Potomac Golf Course, but the underlying issues are quite a bit more important than tree removal.

Reyes’ ruling in the case also sets the stage for possible sanctions against the administration and in particular against Trump DOJ attorneys for their conduct in the case, including possibly misleading the court.

If you have a few extra moments today, the first 6 1/2 pages of Reyes ruling are a tour de force that provide a very good sense of how off the rails things have gotten.

items.title: Dangerous and Absurd: The Story of Donald Trump
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
A Ridiculous Threat to Democracy

Before getting into the state of play in the two major election interference cases in California and Alaska, I want to acknowledge an inherent tension in covering President Trump’s attack on free and fair midterm elections.

It’s a tension that should be familiar to anyone who has lived through the Trump era: The severity of his threat to democracy is matched only by his pure absurdity.

The temptation to pick one lane or the other rather than straddle both lanes is strong. You may want to dismiss the entire midterm attack as an absurd scheme not worthy of you attention; or you may want to light your hair on fire about the coming fascism and ignore the inherent weaknesses in Trump’s desperate effort to stave off a loss of both chambers of Congress.

It’s hard to entertain those competing impulses, but the truth is the attack on the midterms is both dangerous and ridiculous, like Trump himself.

The Latest on California …

: We’re awaiting a decision from the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on the Trump DOJ’s effort to force California to segregate and not yet count mail-in ballots from voters who appear on a dubious administration-generated list of what it claims contains some 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters.

The appeals court took the rare step of hearing oral arguments via Zoom as it considers the Trump DOJ’s long-shot appeal in a case where the lower court hadn’t even ruled yet. At least two judges on the appeals court panel appeared very unlikely to countenance this premature appeal and dismiss it. You can read my full report on the oral arguments here.

: If the 9th Circuit clears the way, as expected, the California case goes back to U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who has an important hearing scheduled for 1 p.m. PT Tuesday. This will be the first time Judge Carter has taken up the case in any meaningful way since it was filed. He’s indicated he will consider all of the pending motions, including the Trump DOJ’s request for an injunction that would immediately require California to segregate some mail-in ballots even as voting is underway. Judge Carter says he will rule “promptly” after the oral arguments. The losing side will undoubtedly appeal his decision back to the 9th Circuit.

: With the news Friday that the Trump DOJ sent letters to every county election official in California threatening them with criminal prosecution if they count mail-in ballots from its list, it’s now clearer that the stakes go beyond the Los Angeles County case and will have immediate statewide implications. If the Trump DOJ manages to prevail in California, it’s hard to imagine it not trying to extend its scheme to other states.

The Trump DOJ’s over-the-top effort to keep Alaska from certifying the election results of its U.S. Senate race is moving quite a bit slower than the California case.

It’s not clear from the docket that the Alaska state defendants have been served the lawsuit yet. In any event, they haven’t responded yet or even had attorneys enter their appearances.

A slew of intervenors opposed to the Trump DOJ’s lawsuit have already sought to participate in the case. One pair of intervenors — the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Alaskans For Mary (Peltola, the Democratic nominee) — has tentatively filed a motion to dismiss the Trump DOJ lawsuit and is asking for expedited rulings in the case.

Since we last checked in on Friday, President Trump brazenly announced that he ordered the DOJ to file the Alaska lawsuit, which is being widely panned by legal experts as flimsy and frivolous.

Experts Weigh in on Election Interference

The Department of Justice is putting its formidable thumb on next week’s elections in a way that seems clearly intended to call into question the legitimacy of any result that is especially unfavorable to Republicans—before those results have even come in. These efforts are incredibly dangerous to our democracy— to the extent that they are legally baseless. And they ought to be loudly and publicly condemned by anyone who cares seriously about democratic legitimacy.

Of the many things that could go wrong in November, I worry most about DOJ seeking to interfere with the tabulation and certification process, especially in a place like Alaska that may determine which party controls the United States Senate. The situation in Alaska is specifically frightening. Due to its complex voting procedures, strange time zone, and remoteness, in normal years it can take a particularly long time to count all of Alaska’s ballots. These types of delays are what Trump has seized on in the past to most successfully attack elections, specifically the COVID-delayed election counts of 2020. I am particularly concerned DOJ could try to seize ballots or voting machines.

The Justice Department is sharply intensifying efforts to intervene in the midterm elections, goaded by a president unfettered by even the limited restraints of his first term.

The next several weeks represent a critical moment for federal law enforcement, a test of whether a department repurposed by President Trump as an instrument of unmediated executive power will be effectively mobilized as a guarantor of his political power.

More Blanche on TV, Please

  • DOJ forced to withdraw its own claim of compliance: After ICE wrongfully deported two more asylum seekers, the Trump DOJ was forced to withdraw its previous claim that the administration was in compliance with court orders in the case, the long-running class action settlement involving unaccompanied minors seeking asylum. The administration has already been held in contempt in the Baltimore case multiple times.

  • U.S. attorney scheme update: The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals offered few clues on how it might rule during oral arguments Friday in the lawsuit by court-appointed U.S. Attorney Roger Rogoff of Seattle, who was fired by the Trump DOJ. Rogoff is challenging the president’s power to fire court-appointed acting U.S. attorneys — a key element of President Trump’s scheme to install loyalists as the top prosecutors in blue states.

  • Woodward seeks recusal of Minnesota judges: Stan Woodward, the No. 3 official in the Trump DOJ, is seeking the recusal of two federal judges in Minnesota who were among those interviewed by the NYT in the aftermath of Operation Metro Surge. Woodward, who already filed a judicial ethics complaint with the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals about the judges who spoke to the NYT, is seeking the recusal of former Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz in a habeas case and U.S. District Judge John Tunheim in a noncitizen voting prosecution. (h/t Marcy Wheeler)

President Trump’s closing argument in the midterm elections is pure undiluted racism, falsely accusing Abdul El-Sayed of being a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” and continuing to assail Somali Americans as congenitally stupid yet smart enough to hack the American dream at the expense of “real” Americans:

Inside the Cheesecake Factory

items.title: Trump DOJ Plays Dirty Pool In California Election Case
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
In its attack on the midterm elections in California, the Trump DOJ has taken an extraordinary new step that exemplifies how far off the rails it has gone under Trump II.

I mentioned yesterday that the Trump DOJ was seeking an immediate ruling on its emergency application for a temporary restraining order to force Los Angeles County to segregate and not count certain alleged noncitizen ballots. As I noted then, the Trump DOJ request for a ruling from the court by noon yesterday came the judge in the case had already set a hearing on the TRO application for next Tuesday.

They appeared to have settled that.

But by the end of the day yesterday, the Trump DOJ appealed what it claimed was the lack of a ruling from the judge, making the astounding assertion his “silence” amounted to a “constructive denial” of its application for a TRO.

It’s hard to convey to non-lawyers how wacky this is — on so many levels — but let’s start with the claim that the judge had been silent.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter was assigned the case just before noon Wednesday morning. About four hours later, he granted an already-pending request from the Trump DOJ to exceed the court’s page limit for its legal memorandum in support of its TRO application. A couple of hours after that, the Trump DOJ formally filed its TRO application.

Sometime after 6:14 p.m. PT, when the the Trump DOJ filed its TRO application, Judge Carter issued an order setting a hearing on the TRO application for Tuesday, Oct. 27 at 1 p.m. ET.

At 8:57 p.m. PT, the Trump DOJ for the first time asked for an expedited ruling by noon PT on Oct. 22. By then, Judge Carter had already set a hearing for next Tuesday.

Noon yesterday came and went without any new ruling from Carter so before the end of the day, the Trump DOJ moved to appeal the case on spurious constructive denial grounds.

How the Trump DOJ construes Judge Carter setting a hearing on its TRO as “silence” is mystifying.

But it actually gets worse.

In its notice of appeal to Judge Carter, the Trump DOJ outlines the sequence of events leading up to what it deems his “constructive denial” but that he had already scheduled a hearing on the TRO. (The appeal isn’t showing up yet on the Ninth Circuit docket so I can’t confirm whether the Trump DOJ played hide the ball with the appeals court on this, too.)

There’s more to say on this, but first here’s a timeline I put together of the key filings and court orders to help orient you:

(Derived from the court docket as it appears on Pacer; exact times from Courtlistener)

: Trump DOJ files its lawsuit against California

: Trump DOJ files a motion to exceed the page limit in its application for a TRO, which it attaches as an exhibit

: The case is assigned to U.S. District Judge John W. Holcomb

: The case is reassigned to U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, a Clinton appointed, because it’s related to an existing case he’s already hearing. (This was a win for California, which had sought the move, and a loss for the Trump DOJ, which had sought assignment to a Trump appointee overseeing a different case that it argued was more related.)

: Just four hours after being assigned the case, Judge Carter grants the Trump DOJ’s motion to exceed the page limit in its application for a TRO

(exact time the order was issued is unclear): Judge Carter schedules a hearing on the Trump DOJ’s application for a TRO for Tuesday, Oct. 27 at 1 p.m. PT

: Trump DOJ files its request for an expedited ruling on its application for a TRO by noon PT on Oct. 22

: Trump DOJ notifies Judge Carter that it is appealing his failure to rule on its application for a TRO by noon, claiming “the Court’s silence is a constructive denial”

Bad DOJ Lawyering All the Way Down

The Trump DOJ’s “constructive denial” argument is the most egregious, but it’s not its only questionable conduct in the case:

  • Five days elapsed after it filed its lawsuit and before it first sought a TRO. Under these circumstances, that delay doesn’t convey the sense of extreme urgency that the Trump DOJ is now insisting the case deserves.

  • It didn’t ask for an expedited ruling in its initial TRO application either (although it was arguably implied by the nature of the filing ).

  • It didn’t engage at all with Judge Carter’s order scheduling a hearing for next Tuesday.

It’s a helluva way to greet a judge who’s been on what is a big, national, high-profile case for all of 28 hours.

“To say this is irregular is an understatement,” writes election law expert Rick Hasen. “I’m not aware of any case where a party, much less the DOJ, sought to appeal a district court’s failure to quickly enough schedule a hearing on a TRO when a hearing had already been set.”

This morning, the Trump DOJ filed a new application for a preliminary injunction (as opposed to a temporary restraining order), trying to take another bite at the apple of getting an immediate ruling from Judge Carter.

Don’t Lose the Forest for the Trees

All of the above procedural wrangling in the California case is only of note because it is part of the Trump administration’s unprecedented attack on the midterm elections. I’ve mostly tried to avoid getting down into the nitty gritty of civil procedure in this case, but the latest Trump DOJ moves are too egregious to ignore, especially given the context.

For my earlier big picture overviews of the case, you can pick from:

Trump DOJ Sues to Block Certification of Alaska Senate Election

Within a few hours of Attorney General Todd Blanche denying that he had any plan to block state’s from certifying the results of the midterms elections, his Justice Department filed a new lawsuit to block Alaska from certifying the U.S. Senate election there — one of the key races that will decide control of the upper chamber.

The Trump DOJ is jumping in before Election Day to try to salvage the re-election of Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R), who is facing former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) and a spoiler candidacy by the similarly named Dan J. Sullivan.

“The sole purpose of his candidacy is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan,” the Trump DOJ claims in its lawsuit.

It’s not at all clear that DOJ has a proper legal basis to bring such a lawsuit, and what it’s seeking in court is disturbingly vague and open-ended: prevent Alaska election officials from certifying the results of the Senate election “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan.”

How it would be determined that ballots were mistakenly cast for the wrong Dan Sullivan is not clear, either.

The lawsuit is signed by Stanley Woodward, Jr., the No. 3 official at DOJ.

items.title: Your Election Interference Fears Were 100% Justified
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
This Is Not a Drill … Repeat … NOT a Drill

The Trump administration has launched a full-blown attack on the midterm elections in California. It’s the very thing that everyone has been worrying that Trump would do for more than a year and yet … it doesn’t feel like the totality of what’s happening has really sunk in or embedded itself in the national political conversation as we sit here 12 days out from the end of voting.

To recap for those just joining us, the Trump administration has used the false pretext of rampant noncitizen voting to:

  • gin up criminal prosecutions nationwide against noncitizens for alleged voting-related crimes, with a special focus on California, where it rolled out a bunch of dubious new charges with high-profile arrests and official press conferences two weeks before the election;

  • sue California to force it to segregate and mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters until it undertakes some new, uncertain, and open-ended investigation into whether the voters are citizens;

  • send federal agents door-to-door looking for noncitizen voters in what is at best a fishing expedition and at worst a campaign to terrorize and instill fear in potential voters in minority communities.

All of this happening — and I cannot emphasize it enough — universal mail-in voting is already underway in California.

The various ways in which the Trump administration spent the past several months trying to monkey with the midterms — asserting unprecedented federal control over state-run federal elections, attempting to use the Postal Service to throttle mail-in ballot delivery, demanding access to voter rolls and individual voter information; marshaling federal databases in a purported effort to ferret out noncitizen voters; among other things — was merely a prelude to its open attack on the midterms now ongoing in California.

The breadth and persistence of those earlier efforts by the administration has probably dulled the senses a bit and made it harder to distinguish what it happening now as a more serious and immediate threat to free and fair elections. The other complicating factor is that the fight to fend off the administration’s attack in California stretches from coast to coast, making it harder for reporters to cover it as a single unified story and for the public to grasp the various tendrils.

There’s a major civil lawsuit underway in California and two separate important lawsuits in D.C. Plus the myriad criminal cases in California, which won’t be decided until after the election. At the same time, federal grand jury subpoenas are still outstanding that demand voter information from California election officials. And amidst all of that the Trump DOJ continues to actively threaten California election officials with prosecution if they don’t capitulate to administration demands.

None of this is how the Justice Department behaved in the run up to past elections — quite the opposite.

None of this is how to run an election.

Drilling Down Into the Details

I hope you’re still with me!

Above is the high level view of the battlefield. If you only take away that broad impression, it’s all good.

But of course, I want to dig down into all the specifics and give you updates on each front in this battle so you know exactly what you need to follow this closely. I’ll still try to keep it manageable in these next few items.

More Threats From the Trump DOJ

I hadn’t zeroed in on this until yesterday, but in the litigation between the Trump DOJ and California, it emerged that acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, the No. 2 official, sent another letter last Friday containing an array of new threats against California election officials:

The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime—and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful. Under 18 U.S.C. § 611(a), noncitizens are prohibited from voting in any election involving federal offices. Under 18 USC. § 2, anyone who aids, abets, ‘counsels, induces, or procures the commission of a federal offense is equally liable. If persons: knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors: to a federal crime.

Administrative difficulty is not a defense to violating federal law or aiding or abetting a federal offense.

The Department strongly urges the County and the SOS to reconsider their positions before taking actions that risk significant federal scrutiny and legal exposure.

As California subsequently told a court, election officials are being asked to conduct the midterm elections under the threat of criminal prosecution from the federal government.

DOJ Is Running Out of Time

In the main case in California, where the Trump DOJ is suing to force California to segregate and not count mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters, both sides are seeking quick rulings.

  • The Trump DOJ wants a TRO issued by noon PT .

  • For now, the federal judge has set a hearing on the Trump DOJ’s TRO request for next Tuesday, Oct. 27. (The judge set this hearing before the Trump DOJ asked for a ruling by noon today.)

With voting ending in 12 days, the timeframes are tight under every scenario. But they’re slightly tighter for the Trump DOJ, assuming it wants to get this case to the Supreme Court in an emergency posture before Election Day, a fair assumption.

Meanwhile, in D.C. Federal Court …

U.S. District Judge James Boasberg is overseeing two separate but related cases that are challenging more broadly aspects of the Trump administration’s attack on the midterm elections. As of yesterday, Judge Boasberg put one of those cases on an expedited pre-election timeline similar to the California case. The other case, just filed on Tuesday, isn’t moving as quickly yet, but it may.

I’m sparing you details on these cases until they ripen a bit more.

Judge Halts DHS Voter Fraud Ops

In yet another case, a federal judge in California blocked DHS from carrying out field operations focused on uncovering voter fraud in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. The order is to remain in place until the polls close on Nov. 3.

The judge was most concerned with U.S. citizens getting swept up in and being intimidated by the DHS field ops, so she blocked ops when they are “likely to involve” people who DHS agents “know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens.”

That leaves some wiggle room for DHS to exploit.

The judge’s ruling came the same day that CBS News reported that armed and uniformed DHS agents have have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status, in an operation that ramped up beginning in September.

“[T]he public’s interest in safe elections, free from interference or intimidation, far exceed Defendants’ purported interest in combating unlawful voting by non-U.S. citizens,” U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguin wrote.

While the California battlefront is the most urgent and pressing threat to the midterms, I would still assess as low the Trump administration’s chances of ultimately prevailing in court. But that doesn’t mean it can’t win. And even more importantly, the fight itself is part of the point and is doing real damage right now by actually interfering in an ongoing election.

Third Country Removal Update

Updates on a couple of the most egregious third country removals that I’ve mentioned over the last couple of months:

  • : A federal judge in California has confirmed that a wrongfully deported Nigerian national is back in the United States after she ordered the Trump administration to facilitate his return. Etinosa Osahon — who was legally barred from being deported to Nigeria because he had already been tortured twice there and was at risk of future torture — was wrongfully deported in May to Ghana, which promptly attempted to transfer him to Nigeria. He refused to continue on the overland journey and was dumped en route in Togo, where he had remained in hiding.

  • : A federal judge in Arizona who ordered the Trump administration on Oct. 6 to facilitate the return of an Egyptian national who had been deported to Equatorial Guinea ratcheted up the pressure on the administration to act more quickly to abide by his original order. The new order comes after Gillian Brockell reported that an ICE deportation flight was scheduled to arrive in Equatorial Guinea today but still not retrieve Ahmed Soliman, whose health is reportedly rapidly deteriorating.

The Retribution: Free Press Edition

  • In a retaliatory move, the Trump White House removed Andrew Feinberg, the reporter whom it derided earlier this week as a “Mongoloid moron,” from the out-of-town print pool for President Trump’s trip to Iowa today.

  • In an extraordinary letter, a White House lawyer demanded that Politico retract a series of palace intrigue stories on Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, concluding his letter with this not-at-all-veiled retaliatory threat:

I therefore demand that Politico immediately correct or retract these publications, issue a prominent and public apology to the President of the United States and to Ms. Wiles, and remove the false reporting from your digital archives. Failure to do so or otherwise respond justifying Politico’s publications within 48 hours will prompt an immediate review of Politico’s relationship with the White House, and, of course, consideration of all other appropriate and available legal remedies.

Hegseth Broke Eisenhower’s Globe

The WaPo, with a metaphor for our time: Hegseth wanted Eisenhower’s globe for his office. His staff broke it.

items.title: DOJ’s List of Noncitizen Voters Exposed As Crap
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
The top election official in Los Angeles County has done a preliminary review of the Trump DOJ’s purported list of alleged noncitizen voters and found it to be … shoddy. Surprising absolutely no one.

Out of DOJ’s list of 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters in California, more than 7,000 had Los Angeles County addresses. Dean C. Logan’s office took a sample of 200 of those L.A. voters and found that 1/4 may have been born in the United States, nearly 1/2 were cancelled or inactive voters, and nearly 3/4 had never voted, according to a new court filing:

It’s critically important to frame this properly: Election administrators must always balance making sure ineligible voters don’t vote with assuring that eligible voters aren’t wrongfully denied their right to vote. Make voting rules and regulations too strict and the risk goes up of excluding legitimate voters and not counting their votes.

It’s a balance that Trump and Republicans refuse to strike in their jihad to vilify noncitizen voters and elevate a vanishingly small problem into a reason to distrust election results. It’s telling that they voice more apparent concern about what they call “vote dilution” by noncitizen voting than they do about outright denying U.S. citizens the right to vote and have their vote counted.

In the California case, the shoddy list makes even more stark the incredible demand the Trump administration is suing to impose on the state. It wants California — with voting already underway — to introduce new additional steps into the vote tabulation process: review DOJ’s crap list, segregate all the ballots cast by people on that list, and run a real-time review to confirm whether those voters are citizens. Then — and only then — can California count those ballots.

Note on whom the burden falls here: The Trump administration can supply a flawed and unreliable list, then California — while already conducting a live election — has to run around and jump through the extra hoops that the administration has created for it.

Here’s how a top Los Angeles County election official put it in her own declaration in the case:

Because the County results must be submitted by December 3, 2026, and certified by the State by December 11, 2026, ballots held pending an open-ended federal review may, in practical effect, never be counted. This process would risk disenfranchising voters who are validly registered. The process the DOJ seeks to have the Registrar undertake jeopardizes that core right for potentially thousands of voters, not to mention the finalization of election results, confidence in election results, and the ability to allow new elected officials to be instated in their positions.

I should mention that the administration has offered to “help” California and work together in cooperative fashion to vet the administration’s crappy list, but it’s too precious an offer to need its own debunking:

“We’re not perfect and that’s why we’ve asked California to cooperate with us,” acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a Monday press conference, anticipating exactly what happened yesterday. “These are the ones where we’re kind of the most confident that they are noncitizens.”

“Kind of the most confident.”

Dems Sue Trump for Election Interference

Various Democratic entities filed a new federal lawsuit in D.C. to try to block the worst of President Trump’s attacks on the midterm elections, including his demands to purge voter rolls and not count ballots, his threats against election officials, and his interference in state-run elections:

The Corruption: $50M Woman Edition

Where to even start with this?

The recently remarried Alina Habba, who now goes by Alina Mildon, landed a guaranteed $50 million deal to serve as general counsel of a brand new corporate entity tied to Venezuelan billionaire Julio Herrera Velutini, the NYT reports. Among the lowlights:

  • The company — Concord Partners, LLC — was formed in Florida on Oct. 22, 2025 by Isabela Herrera, 27, the billionaire’s daughter and a U.S citizen.

  • The deal was for $10 million a year for four years, plus bonuses, bringing the total guaranteed compensation to $50 million.

  • Mildon “finalized the deal” while she was still the acting U.S. attorney in New Jersey.

  • Mildon’s start date was Jan. 1, 2026. By then, Mildon was a senior adviser to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, the role she took after being disqualified as U.S. attorney in New Jersey.

  • President Trump pardoned Julio Herrera Velutini on Jan. 15, 2026.

Mildon denies having any role in the pardon.

The timing of this revelation may be connected to the epic ongoing feud between Mildon and Ric Grenell that has produced a sleazefest of competing allegations of off-the-charts corruption.

Russia’s Failed Attack on Germany

This still hasn’t broken through in the U.S., but over the summer, Russia intelligence launched a drone attack on a cargo plane carrying military assistance to Ukraine while it was parked at an airport in eastern Germany. It was the most dramatic of Putin’s provocations against NATO countries which have been on an uptick since that failed attack.

The attack was part of a broader effort to position agents, explosives and weapons across Europe to strike targets supporting Ukraine and sow chaos that could strengthen political opposition to military aid for Kyiv, according to investigators and intelligence officials.

Investigators have uncovered networks smuggling explosives, drones and weapons into the EU, along with safe houses and concealed underground caches near airports, arms manufacturers and other potential targets.

There’s been a lot of chatter lately about whether World War III is already underway. I think that’s overdetermined, but it’s also true that we probably won’t notice until we’re deep into it.

The Independent’s Andrew Feinberg writes about being targeted by President Trump as a “Mongoloid Moron” in the Oval Office yesterday — an outburst that the White House happily touted on social media.

Who Gets to Define We the People?

Jamelle Bouie: “[T]he drive to denaturalize Omar is, by itself, a startling attack on the liberty of all Americans. It’s a move that harks back to the worst of the nation’s past — those moments when the government sought to shape, define and ultimately choose who would be ‘the people’ of the United States.”

In the racist rants of President Trump and his enablers, Somali Americans are both primitives who eat your pets and ingrates who are undeservedly “living the high life” at your expense:

The only consistency is the rancid appeal to every base human emotion.
